text: January, twenty twenty-five. A lab in Hangzhou publishes a paper with a bold claim.
You can teach a model to reason, to write careful working, check itself and fix its mistakes, without ever showing it one example of careful working.
Not one example? Come on.
On a hard competition maths test, its score went from fifteen point six percent to seventy-one.
Okay. That’s... not nothing.
The paper was DeepSeek R1. Today we read it together, in plain words. It’s the blueprint for this course.
How R1 learned to think. Episode two.
The paper describes a little family of models.
R1-Zero: pure practice, from scores alone. No examples first. It’s the proof that the idea works.
R1: the polished version, with a few extra steps to make it readable.
Aww, and the little ones?
The distilled models: small Qwen and Llama models that learned by copying R1’s answers. Keep an eye on them. They’re the twist at the end.
Here’s how R1-Zero was trained. Take maths and coding problems whose answers a computer can check.
Give the model a fixed template. Think first, inside think tags. Then answer, inside answer tags.
So it tells the model where to think... but not how?
Exactly. No example reasoning to copy. It tries each problem many times, every try gets a score, and the high scorers become more likely.
And the scores come from just two rules, both checked by ordinary code.
Accuracy. Is the final answer right? For maths, compare it with the known answer. For code, run the tests.
And format. Is the thinking inside the think tags?
Why not get another AI to judge the answers? Wouldn’t that be smarter?
They chose not to. A model in training hunts hard for anything that scores well, and it can learn to fool a judge AI. That’s called reward hacking. Plain code is cheap, and hard to fool.
The training method is called GRPO. For each question, the model writes a group of answers.
Each one gets scored. The ones that beat the group’s average get pushed up. The ones below it get pushed down.
Ha, like grading on a curve!
Pretty much. We’ll build it from scratch in Module five.
So R1-Zero trains. Score, nudge, repeat. And nobody ever rewards how long an answer is.
So what happened to the length of its answers?
Pause, and have a guess.
B, shorter! Fewer words, less effort, same reward. I’d do that.
Makes sense, but no. It’s C. The answers grew longer, all on their own.
The model discovered that spending more tokens on thinking led to more right answers. And right answers were what got rewarded.
Here’s the shape. This chart is illustrative. It follows the pattern in the paper, not its exact data.
Answers get longer and longer as training goes on.
And partway through, the authors spotted something odd. The model stopped in the middle of a solution, and wrote...
Wait, wait. Wait. That’s an aha moment I can flag here.
Then it went back and re-checked its approach. Nobody taught it to re-check. It showed up because, sometimes, re-checking led to a right answer.
But R1-Zero had a problem. Its working was hard to read, and it switched between English and Chinese mid-thought.
Why would it do that?
Because nothing in its rewards cared about reading well. The model optimizes exactly what you reward, and nothing else.
So for R1, they built a four-stage recipe.
One. A cold start: a small warm-up on thousands of long, readable worked solutions.
Two. Reasoning practice with scores, plus a new reward for sticking to one language.
Did that cost them anything?
A little. Benchmark scores dipped slightly. They kept it anyway, because the output was far easier to read. Rewards are trade-offs.
Three. Generate lots of answers, keep the good ones, and fine-tune on them. Four. One last round of practice, to polish the final assistant.
And now, the twist. The little models.
The authors asked: what if we skip the teacher, and train a smaller model with practice alone? They tried it on a thirty-two billion parameter Qwen.
With practice alone, it scored forty-seven on that hard maths test.
Copying R1’s answers instead, it scored seventy-two point six.
Wait. So copying beat practice? Then why is this course all about practice?
Fair question. You don’t always have a teacher to copy, and practice is how the teacher was made. Later, we do both.
Quick recap.
R1-Zero learned to reason from scores alone. No worked examples.
The scores came from two rules checked by plain code: accuracy, and format.
Its answers grew longer by themselves. And for small models, copying a teacher can beat practice.
Here’s what gets me.
The whole recipe hangs on two tiny rules. Is it right, and is it tidy. And there’s no teacher anywhere.
That’s right. A program hands out every single score.
But how does a program grade a maths answer it doesn’t understand? And what can it grade at all?
That’s the secret ingredient. In the next episode: grading without a teacher.
Open the length and aha chart in the lesson, and find the aha moment yourself.
See you in the next episode!
